stories.title: Honda says its upgraded F1 engine has hit its internal targets ahead of its Zandvoort debut with Aston Martin
stories.what_happened: Honda's trackside general manager and chief engineer **Shintaro Orihara** confirmed the team's upgraded "spec 2" power unit has met its internal performance targets during factory testing, ahead of its planned first appearance at the **Dutch Grand Prix at Zandvoort**. The changes are described as internal engine refinements — better combustion efficiency, reduced friction, and improved lubrication — rather than anything requiring Aston Martin to redesign its car around it. Orihara was cagey about exact specifics, calling some of it "a secret," but confirmed a filming day at the Hungaroring circuit already let both companies gather live data on the new unit ahead of its competitive debut.
key_points: Honda's revamped power unit has **completed factory testing** and hit **"internal targets"** ahead of its public debut at the **Dutch Grand Prix (Aug 21–23)**.
Engineers estimate a gain of roughly **30–50 extra horsepower**, with Aston Martin hoping for about **half a second per lap**.
The upgrade targets **combustion efficiency, friction, and lubrication** — all internal changes, so Aston Martin's **AMR26 car itself won't need reconfiguring**.
A **filming day at the Hungaroring** already gave both teams real data, aimed at avoiding surprises when the engine is raced for real at Zandvoort.

depth.background: 2026 marked a major regulatory shift for Formula 1's engines (power units), and Aston Martin switched suppliers this season — moving from Mercedes engines to a new **works partnership with Honda**, meaning Honda builds the engine specifically around Aston Martin rather than just supplying a customer unit. A new engine supplier relationship typically takes time to mature, and Honda's first major mid-season upgrade is being closely watched as a sign of how competitive that partnership can become.

stories.title: The US National Institutes of Health stops funding research meant to inform policymakers
stories.what_happened: NIH director **Jayanta Bhattacharya** has set out three rules for what the agency will now fund: research must be **'actionable, rigorous, and in scope'** — with 'in scope' defined as serving NIH's own 'mission-relevant' stakeholder groups, a category that **explicitly excludes policymakers and legislators**. In practice, NIH has begun rejecting or stalling grant applications whose main purpose is generating evidence for public-policy decisions, and **dozens of grants are currently in limbo** as a result, according to Nature's reporting. NIH has historically funded prominent studies assessing the health impact of firearm regulation, abortion-access limits and environmental protections — precisely the category of research now being deprioritized. Scientists warn the shift will shrink the independent evidence base lawmakers rely on when writing health-related legislation.
key_points: **NIH director Jayanta Bhattacharya** says the agency will only fund research that is 'actionable, rigorous and in scope' for its **'mission-relevant' stakeholders — which excludes policymakers**.
NIH is now turning away grant applications whose **primary purpose is informing legislators or regulators**, leaving **dozens of in-progress grants in limbo**.
Past NIH-funded policy research has covered the health effects of **firearm regulations, abortion limits and environmental protections** — exactly the kind of study now at risk.
This continues a broader **reshaping of US federal science funding** under the current NIH leadership since early 2025.

depth.background: The NIH is the world's largest public funder of biomedical research, historically distributing over $40 billion a year to universities and hospitals to study everything from cancer biology to how public policy affects public health. A sizeable, often-cited slice of that funding has gone to research specifically designed to give lawmakers and regulators evidence — for instance, whether a state's gun laws changed injury rates, or how environmental rules affect asthma. Since early 2025, NIH leadership has repeatedly narrowed what it considers fundable 'core mission' research, part of a wider push to cut what officials describe as ideologically-driven or advocacy-adjacent science.

stories.title: India's Supreme Court grows from 34 to 38 judges as President Murmu signs off on the expansion
stories.what_happened: President **Droupadi Murmu** signed the **Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Act, 2026** into law, raising the court's sanctioned strength from **34 to 38 judges** (including the Chief Justice of India). Law minister **Arjun Ram Meghwal** introduced the Bill in the Lok Sabha on **July 20**; the Lok Sabha passed it on **August 3**, and the Rajya Sabha returned it on **August 5**, before it went to the President for assent on **August 11**. The Act is treated as effective from **May 16, 2026** — the date the President had already promulgated an ordinance version of the change, ahead of Parliament passing the full law. The government justified the expansion by pointing to **more than 92,000 cases pending** before the Supreme Court as of January 1, 2026, after the court took in 75,410 new cases in 2025 but disposed of only around 65,000. This is the first change to the court's sanctioned strength since 2019.
key_points: President **Droupadi Murmu** has assented to the **Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Act, 2026**, raising the court's sanctioned strength from **34 to 38 judges**, including the Chief Justice.
It's the **first increase since 2019**, when the number (excluding the CJI) rose from 30 to 33.
The government cites **over 92,000 pending cases** as of January 2026 — the court registered **75,410 new cases** in 2025 but disposed of only about **65,000**.
The law is treated as effective from **May 16, 2026**, the date the President first promulgated it as an ordinance, ahead of Parliament formally passing the Bill.
Parliament passed the Bill this month: **Lok Sabha on August 3**, and the **Rajya Sabha returned it on August 5**.

depth.background: India's Supreme Court is the country's final court of appeal and constitutional arbiter, and its sanctioned strength — the maximum number of judges allowed by law — has been raised only a handful of times as caseloads grew, most recently in 2019. More judges lets the court sit as more simultaneous benches, which matters because most of its work happens in small panels of two or three judges hearing thousands of appeals a year, alongside larger constitutional benches for major cases. The government first raised the judge count by **ordinance** — a temporary law the President can issue when Parliament isn't in session — before Parliament converted it into a permanent Act this month.

stories.title: South Africa hand Bjorn Fortuin the white-ball captaincy and blood fresh faces for a Namibia tour
stories.what_happened: Cricket South Africa announced a **15-player squad** for a white-ball tour of Namibia, naming left-arm spinner **Bjorn Fortuin** as captain for a **T20 International tri-series** against Namibia and Zimbabwe (**August 28 to September 6**) followed by a **three-match ODI series** against Namibia (**September 9-13**). Head coach **Shukri Conrad** said the selection prioritizes player management, with the senior Test group rested so it can focus on earning **World Test Championship points** in upcoming assignments instead. The squad blends experienced fringe players with uncapped talent and rising batter **Dewald Brevis**, giving several players their first taste of senior international selection.
key_points: South Africa named spinner **Bjorn Fortuin** as captain of a fresh-faced squad for a white-ball tour of Namibia, including a **T20I tri-series** with Zimbabwe and a separate **three-match ODI series**.
Coach **Shukri Conrad** said the experimental squad reflects **player-management priorities**, with the Proteas' senior focus on earning **World Test Championship points** instead.
The **15-player squad** includes uncapped and fringe players alongside young batter **Dewald Brevis**.
South Africa are the **reigning World Test Champions**, having beaten Australia in the final at Lord's last June — this tour deliberately rests that core group.

depth.background: South Africa's 'Proteas' won the World Test Championship final against Australia at Lord's in mid-2025, and selectors have since prioritized keeping the core Test squad fresh for future WTC cycles rather than over-scheduling them across white-ball tours. Tours to Namibia and Zimbabwe sit lower down cricket's global hierarchy than series against India, Australia or England, making them a natural place to test fringe and uncapped players without risking established stars. Bjorn Fortuin is a left-arm spinner who has played sporadically for South Africa's white-ball sides; handing him the captaincy is itself a notable step up in responsibility.

stories.title: McLaren says there was no single 'turning point' — just a slow climb that now makes it a real Mercedes rival
stories.what_happened: McLaren team principal **Andrea Stella** said he can't point to one specific moment as the season's turning point, despite the team's commanding win at the **Hungarian Grand Prix** that has reshaped the championship picture. Instead, Stella described a **gradual accumulation of understanding** about where the **MCL40** needed development, crediting a forced **month-long break in April** as the moment the team got space to properly analyze performance data and redirect car-development priorities. He separately reflected on the toll of 2025's title fight, saying the team **'could have collapsed'** under that pressure and calling it the year's most important lesson. Despite downplaying any single breakthrough, the scale of McLaren's Hungary win is widely seen — including by rivals — as evidence the team is now a genuine threat to Mercedes' championship lead for the rest of the season.
key_points: McLaren team principal **Andrea Stella** rejected the idea that the team's dominant **Hungarian Grand Prix win** was a single 'turning point' in its 2026 season.
Stella says the improvement came from a **gradual, monthslong process**, starting with a forced **month-long break in April** that let engineers fully reassess the **MCL40**'s development direction.
Despite denying one big turning point, McLaren's margin of victory in Hungary now marks it as a **genuine championship rival to Mercedes**, alongside Ferrari.
Stella separately admitted the team **'could have collapsed'** under the weight of a difficult 2025 title battle, calling that pressure the year's **biggest lesson**.

depth.background: McLaren enters the second half of the 2026 season chasing Mercedes, who lead the constructors' championship after a dominant first half built around drivers Kimi Antonelli and George Russell. McLaren itself came out of a bruising 2025 title fight and has spent 2026 rebuilding competitiveness with a new car, the MCL40. A month-long enforced break in the F1 calendar in April gave every team extra development time — for McLaren, that pause became a chance to step back and rethink where the car needed the most work, rather than chase quick in-season fixes.

stories.title: Liam Lawson says his best-ever F1 season has changed how he thinks about his career, as Red Bull talks loom
stories.what_happened: Lawson says 2026 has been **'by far'** Racing Bulls' strongest season in the current development era, and that his own results — points in all but three Grands Prix, sitting **9th in the drivers' championship** at the summer break — have changed how he thinks about success. He said his F1 ambitions are **no longer fixed on one particular Red Bull seat**, a shift from the mindset that defined his rockier early years in the sport. Lawson expects discussions with Red Bull about his future beyond 2026 to begin **over the summer break**, and said this is the first season he's had a proper, calm pre-season with the team he's still driving for. Complicating the picture, Red Bull's junior program now has **three** promising drivers — including rising F2 star Nikola Tsolov — competing for just two Racing Bulls seats.
key_points: Lawson sits **9th in the drivers' championship** at the summer break, his best F1 season yet
He says his ambitions are **no longer tied to one specific Red Bull seat**
Conversations with Red Bull about his future are expected to begin **over the summer break**
Racing Bulls has had its **strongest development season** in the current F1 era, per Lawson
F2 rookie **Nikola Tsolov's** rise adds competition for a limited number of Red Bull-family seats

depth.background: **Liam Lawson** is a New Zealand driver who races for **Racing Bulls**, Red Bull's second F1 team, which serves partly as a proving ground for drivers hoping to eventually earn a seat at the main Red Bull team. Lawson had a turbulent start to his top-flight career, including a brief, difficult stint at the senior Red Bull squad before being moved back down. Red Bull manages driver careers across its two teams centrally, meaning seat decisions are made from a single talent pool rather than team-by-team.

stories.title: Russia frees ailing ex-US Marine Robert Gilman after 4+ years in prison on disputed charges
stories.what_happened: Russian President **Vladimir Putin** approved a pardon for Gilman on humanitarian grounds, and he was released from custody on **August 11, 2026** — more than four years, or roughly **1,666 days**, after his arrest. Gilman, 32, had reportedly deteriorated badly in custody: his family said he entered a 'dissociative stupor' in late June and was moved from a prison hospital to a psychiatric ward at a civilian hospital in Voronezh. He is being flown to a **US military hospital in Texas** for medical and psychological evaluation. Unlike past headline swaps — such as the 2024 exchange that freed journalist Evan Gershkovich and Paul Whelan — the State Department said Gilman's release involved **no prisoner exchange or other concession** from Washington.
key_points: Putin approved a **humanitarian pardon** for Gilman, ending over **four years** of detention.
Gilman, a **former US Marine and English teacher**, was arrested in Voronezh in **January 2022**.
He was sentenced to **2 years**, then handed an **additional 8-year term** over an alleged assault on prison guards.
His family says he slipped into a '**dissociative stupor**' and was near death after alleged mistreatment.
The State Department says this was **not part of a prisoner swap** — no US concessions were made.

depth.background: Gilman served in the US Marines from 2019 to 2020. He was travelling by train through Russia in January 2022 when he was arrested and accused of assaulting a police officer while drunk — an allegation his family has called false. A Voronezh court sentenced him to two years, then in December added an eight-year term over an alleged assault on prison guards. The **US government formally designated him 'wrongfully detained'**, the label it uses for Americans it believes are held on politically motivated or unjust charges.

stories.title: Verstappen calls on the Dutch government to save the country's motorsport pipeline as Zandvoort's F1 future stays unresolved
stories.what_happened: Ahead of what is expected to be Zandvoort's final Dutch Grand Prix for the foreseeable future (**August 21-23, 2026**), Max Verstappen publicly urged the Dutch government to step up support for the country's motorsport ecosystem — not just the Grand Prix event, but the **karting and junior-racing pipeline** that produces future drivers. He warned that without that structural backing, Dutch motorsport risks a decline similar to **Germany's**, a country that once dominated F1 through Michael Schumacher's era but has since largely fallen off the calendar and lost its production line of top drivers. Verstappen said he does not view the upcoming race as a true 'farewell,' suggesting he believes Zandvoort could return to the calendar in future years if the funding situation changes.
key_points: Verstappen warned Dutch motorsport could **decline like Germany's** without government backing.
This year's Dutch GP, expected to be the **final one at Zandvoort** for now, is in under **two weeks** (Aug 21-23).
Zandvoort's contract with F1 was **not renewed**, leaving the race's return uncertain.
Verstappen wants **structural investment** in karting and junior racing, not just the Grand Prix itself.
He said he does **not see this as a 'farewell'** and hopes Zandvoort returns to the calendar later.

depth.background: The Dutch Grand Prix returned to F1's calendar in 2021 after a 36-year absence, riding a wave of national enthusiasm for local hero **Max Verstappen**, a multiple world champion. Zandvoort's contract with F1 has now lapsed without renewal, meaning the August 21-23, 2026 race is set to be the track's last for the foreseeable future. Verstappen has been the face of Dutch motorsport's revival and is now using that platform to push for support beyond just the top-level race itself.

stories.title: Barbados Tridents edge Jamaica Kingsmen by 5 runs in tight CPL opener at Sabina Park
stories.what_happened: Barbados Tridents beat hosts Jamaica Kingsmen by **5 runs** in the 4th match of the 2026 Caribbean Premier League at **Sabina Park, Kingston**, on **August 11**. Batting first, the Tridents posted **206/3** from their 20 overs, built around a strong middle-overs platform. Chasing 207 to win, Jamaica Kingsmen fought hard but finished on **201/9**, falling **5 runs** short despite a late push. Fast bowler **Daniel Sams** was the difference-maker with the ball, taking **4 wickets for 20 runs** to restrict Jamaica's chase, and was named Player of the Match.
key_points: Barbados Tridents posted **206/3** and held on to beat hosts Jamaica Kingsmen by **5 runs** in Kingston.
Jamaica Kingsmen fell just short, finishing on **201/9** from their 20 overs.
Fast bowler **Daniel Sams** was named Player of the Match for figures of **4/20**.
It's the Tridents' first outing under their restored name, after the Barbados franchise reverted from "Royals" back to **Barbados Tridents** for the 2026 CPL season.

depth.background: The **Caribbean Premier League (CPL)** is the Caribbean's top T20 franchise tournament, running since 2013 and featuring six regional teams stocked with international stars during the Northern Hemisphere's cricket off-season. Barbados's team has changed names before — it was the Tridents in the league's early years before being rebranded the Royals — and the CPL confirmed the **Tridents** name was restored for 2026. Jamaica's franchise, meanwhile, enters this season under a new **Kingsmen** identity, and both teams are opening their campaigns in a tournament where net run rate often decides who reaches the playoffs.

stories.title: Colombia's earthquake death toll surges past 220 as new president says 5,000 homes destroyed
stories.what_happened: The death toll from Sunday's magnitude-7.4 earthquake in western Colombia has climbed to at least **224**, according to a CNN tally, up from roughly 160 a day earlier as rescuers push into harder-to-reach areas. President De La Espriella said in a national briefing that **700 people were injured** and an estimated **5,000 homes** were damaged or destroyed. First responders pulled a woman alive from the rubble of a collapsed building in Cali nearly **30 hours** after the quake hit, one of several dramatic rescues that have kept hope alive even as the toll rises. Colombia's Geological Service has logged more than 70 aftershocks since the main quake, complicating rescue work and unnerving residents already living outdoors. Seven airports have suspended operations and hospitals, roads, aqueducts, power and telecoms remain disrupted across the hardest-hit cities, all of which remain under the country's highest-level red alert.
key_points: Confirmed deaths have risen to at least **224**, up from ~160 a day earlier, as rescue teams reach more remote towns.
President **Abelardo De La Espriella**, newly inaugurated, says **700 people** were injured and an estimated **5,000 homes** damaged or destroyed.
A woman was pulled alive from a collapsed building in **Cali** almost **30 hours** after the quake struck.
Colombia's Geological Service has recorded more than **70 aftershocks** since the magnitude-7.4 quake.
**Seven airports** remain shut and hospitals, roads and power are disrupted across the hardest-hit region.

depth.background: A magnitude-7.4 earthquake struck western Colombia on Sunday, with the epicenter near San Jose del Palmar, flattening buildings across Pereira, Cali, Quibdo, Manizales and Armenia. All five cities remain under Colombia's highest disaster classification, **'red alert.'** Colombia sits atop the Pacific 'Ring of Fire,' where the Nazca oceanic plate grinds beneath South America, making it one of the most earthquake-prone countries on the continent. The disaster is one of the first major tests for **President Abelardo De La Espriella**, who was only recently inaugurated.

thread.previously: We reported the death toll had climbed past 160 as rescuers dug through rubble after Sunday's magnitude-7.4 earthquake in western Colombia.

stories.title: Israel and Venezuela restore consular ties after a 17-year diplomatic freeze
stories.what_happened: Israel and Venezuela announced on **Tuesday, August 11** that they had agreed to **renew consular relations** after 17 years without formal ties. The agreement, reached after weeks of talks between Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar and Venezuelan Foreign Minister Félix Plasencia, establishes a **coordination mechanism** that will let both countries provide consular services — passports, documentation, and citizen assistance — to their nationals. It stops short of restoring **full diplomatic relations** (embassies and ambassadors), but it is the first official, on-the-record cooperation channel between the two governments since 2009. The thaw follows Israel sending an **aid and disaster-response delegation** to Venezuela in June after twin earthquakes killed thousands, and comes months after the **US toppled Maduro** in a January raid.
key_points: Israel and Venezuela agreed to **renew consular relations**, 17 years after Venezuela cut ties over Gaza.
The deal creates a **coordination mechanism** for consular services — short of full diplomatic relations.
It follows Israel sending an **aid and disaster-response team** to Venezuela after June's twin earthquakes.
It also follows the **US toppling of Nicolás Maduro** in a January 2026 military raid, with interim leader **Delcy Rodríguez** now under heavy pressure from Washington.
Talks were led by Israeli Foreign Minister **Gideon Saar** and Venezuelan counterpart **Félix Plasencia**.

depth.background: Venezuela severed relations with Israel **17 years ago**, under Hugo Chávez, in protest of Israeli military operations in the Gaza Strip — part of a broader anti-US, anti-Israel foreign policy stance that Chávez and later Nicolás Maduro maintained for nearly two decades. That changed dramatically in **January 2026**, when a US military raid toppled Maduro's government; interim president **Delcy Rodríguez** now runs the country under sustained pressure from President Trump to realign Venezuela's foreign policy with Washington's interests, including its energy and diplomatic priorities.

stories.title: Google's Gemini app crosses 1 billion monthly users, closing in on ChatGPT
stories.what_happened: Pichai said on **August 11** that the standalone Gemini app has surpassed **1 billion monthly active users**, calling it one of the company's **fastest-growing products** and the **14th Google product** to hit that scale (alongside Search, Gmail, Maps, YouTube and others). The growth curve has been steep: Gemini had roughly **400 million** monthly users in May 2025, **900 million** a year later, and **950 million** by its most recent quarterly earnings call before crossing the billion mark now. Google also said **daily active users have tripled** over the past year, suggesting people aren't just trying Gemini once but returning to it regularly. The milestone lands just weeks after ChatGPT itself crossed 1 billion monthly users, effectively pulling the two biggest consumer AI products into a **dead heat on raw reach**, even though usage intensity and revenue between them can still differ sharply.
key_points: Google CEO **Sundar Pichai** announced Gemini has passed **1 billion monthly active users**.
It is the **14th Google product** ever to reach the 1-billion-user mark.
Users have **more than doubled in about a year** — Gemini had **400 million** users in May 2025.
Daily active users have **tripled over the past year**, a faster growth rate than the monthly figure alone shows.
The milestone puts Gemini roughly level with **OpenAI's ChatGPT**, which crossed 1 billion monthly users in June 2026.

depth.background: For most of the generative-AI boom that started in late 2022, **ChatGPT** was the runaway leader in consumer AI apps, with Google's Gemini (and its earlier Bard branding) playing catch-up. Google's advantage has always been distribution: Gemini is built into **Android phones, Search, Gmail, and Workspace**, giving it a shortcut to huge user numbers that a standalone app like ChatGPT doesn't have. Over the past 18 months Google has leaned harder into that advantage, pushing Gemini prompts and summaries directly into products **billions of people already use daily**.

stories.title: Max Verstappen's Red Bull exit clause activates, making him F1's biggest free agent
stories.what_happened: Reports on **August 11** confirmed that Max Verstappen is now, in practical terms, a **free agent**: his Red Bull contract's exit clause — triggered by his position outside the **top two** in the drivers' standings when the season entered its summer break — is now active, meaning he can negotiate with rival teams without breaching his contract. Verstappen currently sits behind championship leader **Kimi Antonelli** and has been unable to close the gap as Red Bull's **RB22** has lagged rivals. **Mercedes and McLaren**, the two strongest teams this season, are seen as the most realistic destinations if he decides to leave. It follows Wednesday's news that F1 commercial boss **Stefano Domenicali** had held 'constructive' talks with Verstappen about staying in the sport beyond 2026 — talks that now look more like an attempt to keep him at Red Bull specifically, or in F1 at all, rather than assuming his loyalty.
key_points: Verstappen's **Red Bull contract runs to 2028**, but contains an **exit clause tied to championship position**.
The clause **activated on August 11** because he was outside the **top two** in the standings entering the summer break.
**Mercedes and McLaren** are named as the teams best placed to make a move, given their current competitiveness.
Verstappen has **four F1 world titles** and is widely rated the best driver on the current grid.
Red Bull is currently **fourth in the constructors' standings**, over 200 points behind leaders Mercedes.

depth.background: Modern F1 driver contracts increasingly include **performance-linked exit or release clauses**, which let a top driver leave a struggling team without penalty if the car isn't competitive enough — protecting the driver's title chances from being tied to a team's bad car. Verstappen has won **four consecutive world championships** with Red Bull (2021–2024) but the team has struggled to adapt to F1's new 2026 technical rules, with its **RB22 car** reportedly regarded internally as underperforming. Speculation about Verstappen's future has simmered for much of the season as Red Bull's competitiveness has slipped.

thread.previously: Yesterday, F1 commercial boss Stefano Domenicali said he'd held 'constructive' talks with Verstappen about the four-time champion staying in the sport beyond 2026, amid swirling questions about his future.
thread.changed: Today it emerged the situation is more urgent than 'talks about staying': Verstappen's contract, which runs through 2028, contains a **performance exit clause** that has now formally activated because he entered the summer break outside the top two in the standings — making him a free agent other teams can legally approach.

stories.title: Wall Street slips from record highs as Brazil's cooling inflation reopens the door to a rate cut, gold jumps
stories.what_happened: Data released this week showed Brazil's **IPCA inflation index rose just 0.03% month-on-month in July**, cooling the annual rate to **4.4%**, down from 4.6% in June and matching economist forecasts. Food inflation, a key driver of the recent overshoot, **eased for a second straight month to 3.4%** year-on-year. The reading put headline inflation back within the central bank's target band for the first time in two months, and analysts said it **opens room for a 25-basis-point cut** at the bank's September meeting. Against that backdrop, US stocks were mixed: the **S&P 500 dipped 0.06% to 7,753**, a small pullback from recent record levels, while the **dollar index rose 0.21% to 99.748** as traders pared expectations for near-term rate cuts elsewhere. **Gold gained 1.40% to $4,402 an ounce**, a move consistent with investors adding safe-haven hedges even as headline risk appetite looked calm.
key_points: The **S&P 500 slipped 0.06% to 7,753**, pulling back slightly after recent record highs.
Brazil's July inflation (IPCA) cooled to **4.4% year-on-year**, down from **4.6% in June** — a three-month low.
The reading pulled inflation **back inside Brazil's central bank target range** (3%, plus or minus 1.5 points), opening the door to a **possible 25-basis-point rate cut in September**.
The **dollar index climbed 0.21% to 99.748** as traders trimmed bets on near-term rate cuts elsewhere.
**Gold jumped 1.40% to $4,402/oz** as investors leaned toward safety amid the mixed signals.

depth.background: Brazil's central bank, like most, sets an inflation target and adjusts its benchmark **Selic rate** to hit it — cutting rates to stimulate a slowing economy once inflation looks under control, and holding or raising them when prices are running hot. Brazilian inflation had spent two straight months above the top of that target band, driven largely by food prices, which kept the central bank cautious about cutting rates. Global investors watch emerging-market inflation prints like Brazil's IPCA (Índice de Preços ao Consumidor Amplo, the country's main consumer price index) closely because they shift bets on capital flows into or out of emerging-market bonds and currencies, which in turn ripple into the dollar and safe-haven assets like gold.

stories.title: Hackers used a hijacked private cellular network to sabotage a second Polish power plant
stories.what_happened: CERT Polska published a follow-up report revealing that attackers first broke into a wind farm's internet-exposed **Fortinet VPN/firewall device** — equipment meant to let remote staff securely log in. From there, they used a cellular router (a Teltonika device) to tunnel via SSH into the electricity distribution operator's **private APN** — a dedicated mobile network utilities use to remotely manage grid equipment, normally isolated from the public internet. Once inside, the attackers moved laterally into the heating plant's operational-technology network and targeted a **Wago programmable logic controller (PLC)** — the industrial computer that directly controls physical equipment. CERT Polska says the root cause was a common misconfiguration letting any device inside a private APN talk to any other device on it, meaning many other utilities — in Poland and beyond — could share the same weakness.
key_points: Poland's national cyber authority, **CERT Polska**, revealed a previously undisclosed **December 2025** attack on a heating plant serving **50,000 residents**.
Attackers pivoted through a wind farm's **VPN firewall**, then a cellular router, into the utility's **private mobile network (APN)** to reach the plant's control systems.
It's the first documented attack of its kind against European energy infrastructure — a technique never seen before.
CERT Polska says the underlying misconfiguration is **common across Poland and likely used internationally**.
The full investigation took **over three months**, which is why it wasn't in the original report on Poland's wave of energy-sector attacks.

depth.background: In late 2025, Poland's wind, solar, and heating infrastructure was hit by a wave of coordinated cyberattacks, which CERT Polska — Poland's national Computer Emergency Response Team, the government body that investigates and discloses major cyber incidents — reported on at the time. What's new today is a deep-dive follow-up on one specific incident left out of that first report because it took **three months to fully analyze**: a December 29, 2025 attack on a combined heat and power (CHP) plant supplying heating to about **50,000 people**. The attack used a genuinely novel path into the plant's industrial control systems — the computers that physically operate equipment like valves and generators — that security researchers hadn't documented before.

stories.title: Leclerc demands Ferrari investigate wild swings in race pace, as Hamilton's influence behind the scenes grows
stories.what_happened: Charles Leclerc is publicly demanding Ferrari investigate why the SF-26 has shown such wildly inconsistent race pace, saying: **'out of the last three races, there were two races where we were expecting to struggle, and we finished first and second... in the race where we expected to do well, we finished fourth and fifth.'** Separately, former F1 driver and pundit Damon Hill said Lewis Hamilton's behind-the-scenes influence has been central to Ferrari's 2026 turnaround — Hamilton reportedly sent the technical team documents describing changes he wanted, which he describes as 'ideas' rather than 'orders,' and pushed Ferrari toward the **Carbon Industrie** brake supplier he used at Mercedes. Leclerc later switched to the same Carbon Industrie brakes himself, after blaming his previous Brembo brakes for his crash at Monaco.
key_points: Charles Leclerc is demanding Ferrari **investigate its SF-26's inconsistent race pace** after wildly swinging results.
In the last three races, Ferrari finished **1st and 2nd** in two it expected to struggle in — then **4th and 5th** in one it expected to lead.
Ex-F1 driver Damon Hill says Lewis Hamilton has effectively **taken control** of Ferrari's technical direction behind the scenes.
Hamilton reportedly pushed Ferrari toward the **Carbon Industrie brake supplier** he used at Mercedes.
Leclerc later switched to the **same brakes** after blaming his old Brembo setup for his **Monaco crash**.

depth.background: Ferrari's Formula 1 team has spent years trying to close the gap to Red Bull and Mercedes, and 2026 brought a major shake-up when seven-time champion Lewis Hamilton joined the team from Mercedes, pairing with Charles Leclerc, Ferrari's long-time lead driver. Hamilton is known not just for his driving but for the deep technical influence he built at Mercedes during his championship years there, working closely with engineers on car setup and development. How much input a driver should have over engineering decisions — versus deferring entirely to the technical team — is a long-running tension in F1, especially when a superstar driver joins a team with its own established way of doing things.

stories.title: Shiprocket sets IPO price band at ₹92-97, aiming to raise ₹1,617 crore in its e-commerce logistics debut
stories.what_happened: Shiprocket has set its IPO price band at **₹92 to ₹97 per share**, valuing the **₹1,617.48 crore** issue. The IPO opens for subscription on **August 12** and closes **August 14**, with a minimum lot size of **154 shares** (about ₹14,938 for retail investors at the upper band). Shares are expected to list on the BSE and NSE around **August 19**. Shiprocket is the latest name in an already packed IPO week in India, alongside Milky Mist Dairy Food, Dhoot Transmission, Molbio Diagnostics and Behari Lal Engineering — **five mainboard IPOs** together aiming to raise over ₹7,400 crore.
key_points: Price band set at **₹92-97 per share**, valuing the issue at **₹1,617.48 crore**
IPO opens **August 12**, closes August 14; lists on BSE/NSE around **August 19**
Minimum lot size **154 shares** — about ₹14,938 for retail investors at the upper band
Backed by **Temasek**, Singapore's state investment fund
One of **five mainboard IPOs** opening this week, together targeting over ₹7,400 crore

depth.background: Shiprocket built its business helping small and mid-sized online sellers — the kind who can't negotiate their own courier deals — access shipping, warehousing and logistics tools, riding India's e-commerce boom over the last decade. Its backers include **Temasek**, a signal of institutional confidence in India's logistics-tech sector. An **IPO (initial public offering)** lets a private company sell shares to the public for the first time, raising capital and letting early investors exit.

stories.title: Colombia's earthquake death toll climbs past 160 as rescuers keep digging through rubble
stories.what_happened: The confirmed death toll rose to at least **169** people as of Tuesday morning, according to Asocapitales, an association of Colombia's capital cities, up from roughly 132 reported a day earlier. President De La Espriella said in a national briefing that **700 people were injured** and an estimated **5,000 homes** were damaged or destroyed. Rescue teams — aided by police, soldiers, volunteers, dogs and drones — worked through the night with excavators and, at times, bare hands, hunting for survivors beneath rubble in Pereira and Cali. The quake also cracked apart one tower of a historic cathedral in Manizales. Officials say the toll is expected to keep climbing as crews reach areas initially cut off by damaged roads and communications.
key_points: The death toll from Monday's **7.4-magnitude earthquake** has risen to at least **169**, per Colombia's association of capital cities.
**700 people** are injured and an estimated **5,000 homes** were damaged or destroyed, President **Abelardo De La Espriella** said.
Rescue teams are using **dogs and drones** to search for survivors trapped under collapsed buildings in **Pereira and Cali**.
The quake cracked apart a tower of a **historic cathedral** in Manizales and reduced multi-story buildings to rubble.
This is already Colombia's **deadliest earthquake in decades**, and officials expect the toll to keep climbing.

depth.background: A **7.4-magnitude earthquake** struck Colombia's coffee-growing heartland early Monday, centered near the Pacific coast and felt as far as Bogotá. It is the country's strongest quake in years, hitting a densely populated region of mid-sized cities — Pereira, Cali, Manizales — built with a mix of older masonry and modern construction, which is why the death toll and damage have been so severe. **Colombia's newly inaugurated president, Abelardo De La Espriella**, is managing his first major national disaster response just weeks into office. Search-and-rescue operations are always a race against time, since survival rates for anyone trapped under rubble fall sharply after the first 72 hours.

thread.previously: We reported Monday's 7.4-magnitude earthquake had killed at least 132 people across Colombia's coffee-growing region, its deadliest quake in decades.
thread.changed: The confirmed toll has risen to at least 169, with 700 injured and roughly 5,000 homes damaged; the new president gave a national briefing and search teams are still digging through rubble in Pereira and Cali.

stories.title: Bangladesh renews pressure on India to extradite ousted PM Sheikh Hasina
stories.what_happened: Bangladesh's government told India it hopes to see the extradition process for Sheikh Hasina **expedited**, according to reporting confirmed on August 11. The message came during a courtesy meeting between India's High Commissioner to Dhaka, Dinesh Trivedi, and Bangladesh's interim leader Tarique Rahman. Bangladesh also repeated its request for India to hand over individuals accused in the killing of Osman Hadi, a case connected to the 2024 unrest. A Bangladeshi court has already convicted Hasina and her former interior minister in absentia and sentenced them to **death** for crimes against humanity linked to the deadly crackdown on protesters. India has not formally responded to the latest request.
key_points: Bangladesh again asked India to **speed up the extradition** of former PM **Sheikh Hasina**, in hiding in India since 2024.
The request came as India's High Commissioner **Dinesh Trivedi** made a courtesy call on Bangladesh's interim leader **Tarique Rahman**.
Bangladesh also renewed its demand for the return of people accused in the **killing of Osman Hadi**, tied to last year's uprising.
A Dhaka court has already **sentenced Hasina to death in absentia** for crimes against humanity over the crackdown on protesters.
India has so far given **'no comment'**, despite Bangladesh citing a **2013 bilateral extradition treaty**.

depth.background: Sheikh Hasina ruled Bangladesh for 15 years before being toppled in **August 2024** by a student-led uprising against her increasingly authoritarian government. She fled to India, where she has remained ever since, occasionally making public remarks that Dhaka says interfere in Bangladeshi politics. Bangladesh's interim government, now led by Tarique Rahman, has repeatedly demanded her return to face trial, while India — Hasina's longtime regional ally — has neither granted nor formally refused the request, leaving the issue unresolved for nearly two years.

stories.title: India's Parliament logjam deepens as Opposition demands Amit Shah explain police crackdown on NEET protesters
stories.what_happened: Congress MPs moved an **Adjournment Motion** in the Lok Sabha this week, seeking to suspend the House's scheduled business specifically to debate the police response to the **July 20 'Sansad Chalo' march**, where students protesting the NEET paper leak clashed with police at Jantar Mantar. Congress leader **Priyanka Gandhi Vadra** said the deadlock between the Opposition and government "will continue" until Home Minister **Amit Shah** personally makes a statement on the incident. Delhi Police have put the toll from that day's clash at roughly **60 injured protesters** and over **118 injured police personnel**, and contested allegations have circulated that unmarked personnel used excessive force, including against minors. Parliamentary Affairs Minister **Kiren Rijiju** said the government is "ready to discuss" the issue and that Shah will make a statement, but as of **August 11**, the standoff had already eaten into the limited sitting days left before the Monsoon Session's scheduled close on **August 13**, with both Houses repeatedly adjourning amid protests.
key_points: Congress moved an **Adjournment Motion** demanding Home Minister **Amit Shah** make a statement on police action against NEET protesters.
The protest in question: the **July 20 'Sansad Chalo' march** at Jantar Mantar, where police used **lathis and tear gas** on demonstrators.
Delhi Police say around **60 protesters** and over **118 police personnel** were injured that day.
With only a few sitting days left in the **Monsoon Session**, bills on women's reservation, delimitation and the **FCRA** law are stuck behind the standoff.
Parliamentary Affairs Minister **Kiren Rijiju** says the government is ready to let Shah address the House.

depth.background: On **July 20**, thousands of students and youth groups marched on Parliament to protest alleged irregularities and a leak in the **NEET** medical-entrance exam, demanding the education minister's resignation. When protesters pushed past barricades, police responded with lathi charges and tear gas, and both sides accuse the other of provoking the clash, with allegations that some students, including minors, were hurt. The Opposition **INDIA bloc** has used the incident to repeatedly disrupt Parliament's ongoing Monsoon Session, insisting Home Minister Amit Shah personally answer for the police response before other business proceeds — a separate but related flashpoint to this week's Jharkhand exam-protest clash, which is fuelling the same broader standoff.

stories.title: India approves trial run of 1 billion plastic ₹10 and ₹20 notes
stories.what_happened: The Indian government has cleared a plan to print **1 billion polymer banknotes** each in the **₹10 and ₹20** denominations for field trials, Finance Minister **Nirmala Sitharaman** told the Rajya Sabha in a written reply on **August 11**. She said the **Reserve Bank of India** put forward the proposal after its central board recommended testing polymer notes based on how other countries have used them. If the trials go well, polymer notes could later be issued regularly in these denominations, running alongside the existing paper ₹10 and ₹20 notes rather than replacing them immediately. Sitharaman said the procurement process is still at an early stage, so the government cannot yet estimate a launch timeline or the total cost of the switch.
key_points: The government approved printing **1 billion polymer banknotes** each of **₹10 and ₹20** for field trials, Parliament was told.
Finance Minister **Nirmala Sitharaman** confirmed the move in a written reply to the **Rajya Sabha** on **August 11**.
The **RBI's central board** recommended the switch after studying how other countries use polymer notes.
Polymer notes will circulate **alongside** existing paper notes, not replace them outright.
The government says it's **too early** to estimate a launch date or cost, since procurement hasn't started.

depth.background: India currently prints all its currency on cotton-based paper, which wears out faster, is easier to counterfeit and is more vulnerable to moisture than **polymer (plastic) banknotes**, already used for decades by countries like Australia, the UK, Canada and Singapore. The RBI has floated polymer notes before, including a small ₹10 field trial roughly a decade ago in a handful of cities, but never scaled it nationally. Polymer notes typically cost more to produce upfront but last several times longer than paper notes, which can lower costs over their full lifespan and cut down on how often notes need reprinting.

stories.title: Jharkhand exam protest escalates into a Parliament clash after police use water cannons on job aspirants
stories.what_happened: Police in Jharkhand used **water cannons, tear gas and lathi charges** against job aspirants protesting near the state Assembly, in a clash that escalated a recruitment-exam dispute already running for more than two weeks. In response, ruling NDA MPs staged a protest inside Parliament in Delhi on **August 11**, marching from the Parliament Library to the main gate ('Makar Dwar') chanting slogans like 'Rahul Gandhi Jawab Do' ('Rahul Gandhi, answer'). The BJP accused Gandhi of being **'either culpable or incapable'** of acting against the Jharkhand government, and said he was avoiding a parliamentary debate on the student protests. Opposition INDIA-bloc MPs confronted the NDA MPs at Parliament's gate, with security personnel forming a cordon to keep the two groups apart.
key_points: Police used **water cannons, tear gas and lathi-charges** on job aspirants protesting near the Jharkhand Assembly.
The protest is over alleged **irregularities in recruitment exams**, an issue simmering for over two weeks.
Ruling **NDA MPs marched inside Parliament**, chanting slogans demanding Congress leader **Rahul Gandhi** answer for the crackdown.
Jharkhand is run by a Congress-JMM-RJD coalition, which the BJP says is either **'culpable or incapable'** on the issue.
**Opposition INDIA bloc MPs faced off** with NDA MPs at Parliament's main gate, with security forming a cordon between them.

depth.background: This story began when Jharkhand's government agreed to cancel a competitive recruitment exam after mass cheating allegations, but the affected job aspirants kept protesting for over two weeks, saying cancellation alone didn't fix the underlying unfairness in the hiring process. Jharkhand is governed by an opposition INDIA-bloc coalition (Congress, JMM and RJD), which put the state government under the national opposition's political umbrella. That set up a clash with the ruling BJP-led NDA in Delhi, which has used the protests to target Congress leader Rahul Gandhi directly.

thread.previously: Jharkhand's government canceled a tainted competitive recruitment exam after mass cheating allegations, but affected job aspirants kept protesting into a 17th straight day as of August 10, saying the cancellation alone didn't resolve their grievances.
thread.changed: Police used water cannons, tear gas and lathi charges on the protesters, and the confrontation jumped from the streets of Ranchi into Parliament, where ruling NDA MPs staged a floor protest targeting Congress's Rahul Gandhi over the crackdown.
